extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, philosophy, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the substantive criteria that an explanation or theory of humor must satisfy (psychological, physiological, evolutionary, and social). Focus is on what counts as 'humor' or the 'sense of humor' and how to judge competing accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-mixture definition (Hecker / Joubert style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic consists in the simultaneous stimulation, from one source, of two feeling-qualities, pleasure and pain, of approximately equal strength; their equality causes an oscillation of attention back and forth between these feelings, giving the character of an 'intermittent joyful surprise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hecker's formulation: 'a rapid oscillation back and forth between pleasure and pain.' Examples/explanation: this oscillation is likened to alternation between light and dark (Glanz) so that the pleasant side is emphasized. Anti-pattern/limitation: this definition 'rules out that very surplus of pleasure which it is supposed to explain' and cannot plausibly explain why pleasure, and not pain, should be elevated through contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological account of laughter (Hecker's tickling model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter (as in tickling) is explained physiologically: peripheral stimulation leads to sympathetic activity, dilation of pupils, lowered cerebral blood-pressure, diaphragm action, and then compensatory increased thoracic pressure causing laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hecker inferred that intermittent 'joyful surprise' would set in motion the same sympathetic adjustive apparatus as tickling. Limitation noted: 'tickling is a very peculiar form of peripheral stimulation' and laughter follows tickling only in certain moods; the physiology does not fully carry over to the comic even if the psychology remains significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wundt/Kraepelin 'oscillation with pleasure prevailing' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: In the comic, separate ideas entering a perception or thought are partly harmonious and partly contradictory, producing an oscillation of feelings in which the positive side (pleasure) not only prevails but 'gains the mastery' and is 'elevated through the immediate contrast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the 'official deliverance' of German psychology. Critique: merely asserting that pleasure prevails and is elevated does not explain why pleasure, rather than pain, is amplified; requires additional account of equilibrium between feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness/irreducibility of the comic emotion (Lipps)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The feeling of the comic is a feeling of the comic and nothing else' — the comic emotion is unique and not analysable into other emotions like reproach or gratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to separate the comic from other emotions and to satisfy McDougall's first test for instincts (unique emotional quality). This criterion supports treating humor as a primary emotional category rather than a compound of other feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: McDougall's three tests for an instinct (applied to humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: An instinct is identified by: (1) a unique and irreducible quality of emotional excitement; (2) occurrence not only in humans but in higher animals; (3) occasional morbid exaggeration (hypertrophy) in some sane individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to humor: (1) Lipps's uniqueness claim; (2) reports and observations (Darwin, Romanes, Sully) that dogs and some monkeys show rudiments of ludicrous response, though modern comparative psychology is cautious; (3) hysterical/mad laughter and drug-induced comicality (hashish) show morbid intensification. A theory claiming humor is instinctive should address these three tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early spontaneous appearance in children (instinct criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous laughter appears early and spontaneously in infants; we teach children when not to laugh rather than to laugh, indicating an innate disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited: babies smile very early (around 40th day on average), and mimic/masque-style play elicits laughter without instruction. Anti-pattern: if a theory ignores developmental facts or cannot account for infant spontaneity, it is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on playful attitude (reframing pain as amusing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparent pain-source becomes, under a playful attitude, a source of 'emotional interest' that is itself pleasant and greeted with a tendency to laughter; humor functions originally in the state of play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The playful frame transforms stimuli that would otherwise cause pain into sources of amusement. A satisfactory theory must distinguish between genuine pain and play-contextualized 'pain' that yields humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infectiousness via sympathy and suggestion (social contagion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous emotion is highly communicable: hearing or seeing others laugh often produces laughter and humorous emotion even without knowing the cause; suggestion (reputation, atmosphere) can make poor material seem funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: laughing with a group produces enjoyment even if one hasn't heard the joke; the mere report that a great comedian will appear 'sets in action the machinery for enjoying his jokes.' Theories must account for social contagion and atmosphere effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of laughter types (must distinguish causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many different acts/forms of laughter (sexual/hostile glee, laughter from chilliness, fear, hysterical laughter, mimic reflex of idiots, chemical exhilarants, laugh at deliverance from danger, general expression of pleasure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any comprehensive theory should recognize and account for the diversity of laughter forms and not conflate them all under a single mechanism without qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'point' of a joke — simultaneous birth of two feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Hecker: 'The simultaneousness of the birth of the two feelings constitutes the so-called point, without which the comic effect even of a joke or an anecdote is lost.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a joke to have its comic effect there must be that moment ('point') where contradictory feelings arise together; theories of joke structure should identify and explain this moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary plausibility/timing (late-evolving instinct account)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sense of humor is instinctive, it is plausibly a late-evolving trait, valuable only in complex, experimental organisms with extended play periods; therefore absence in many animals does not disprove instinctive status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to rebut opponents who demand that humor-like phenomena appear widely in animals for physiological/release theories. Theories should be consistent with plausible evolutionary history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to explain individual differences (must account for 'no sense of humor')
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful theory must explain why some people 'have no sense of humor' while others are highly humorous; inability to account for such individual differences undermines purely mechanical/release/derision/Freudian accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: some individuals lack humorous response but are proud or well self-possessed; theories must accommodate variability in emotional endowment and temperament.
